editorNote: Commodore is selling an instant office, while Electronic Arts and Sega give the home-computer game shelf fresh reasons to linger.
morningLine: A $300 computer with software in ROM meets $40 strategy games and arcade favorites on disk.

lead.headline: Commodore Readies the Plus/4 for the Holiday Shelf
lead.dek: A $300 “productivity machine” promises an office in ROM, but the C64’s immense game library will not follow it.
body: Commodore’s Plus/4 is moving toward the holiday counter with an unusual pitch for a home computer: useful software is already inside. An October COMPUTE! hands-on report lists the machine at $300 with 64K of RAM and four integrated applications collectively called 3-Plus-1. The magazine’s reporting predates this week, so an exact October 15 launch is not established.

The package, developed by International Tri Micro, puts a word processor, spreadsheet, file manager and business-graphics program in ROM. BASIC 3.5 offers more than 75 commands; the machine can show 320-by-200 high-resolution graphics and 16 colors in eight luminance levels. Commodore calls it “The Productivity Machine,” hoping the buyer will value a ready-made work desk.

But this is no Commodore 64 with office programs added. The Plus/4 lacks the C64’s sprites and SID sound chip and runs practically none of its predecessor’s software. That divides the shop window: a Plus/4 buyer gains integrated work tools but gives up the thickening C64 game shelf that is drawing players to home computers.

The companion Commodore 16, with 16K of memory at a planned $100, is meant to take the VIC-20’s entry-level place. Commodore also planned roughly 30 Plus/4 programs at introduction. Whether a new software line can grow quickly enough is the question this autumn, as Electronic Arts and Sega make the older machines look lively.

stories.headline: Archon II and Skyfox broaden Electronic Arts’ games line
body: Electronic Arts is widening the computer-game counter with Archon II: ADEPT and Skyfox, both listed by October COMPUTE! at a suggested $40. These are same-month product notices, not evidence of an exact-week release.

Archon II brings chesslike strategy into contests over energy points, mixing spellcasting with action encounters on Atari 48K and Commodore 64 machines. Skyfox takes a different course: an Apple II disk game with training missions and 15 combat scenarios. Together they show how varied the home-computer game can be beside a cartridge console.

stories.headline: Spy Hunter and Tapper arrive on home computers
body: Sega’s computer editions of Spy Hunter and Tapper carry two arcade names onto disk and cartridge for Commodore 64, IBM PC and PCjr, Atari and Apple II families, according to October COMPUTE!. Each has a suggested $39.95 price.

Spy Hunter keeps its weapon-equipped driving chase; Tapper brings four bar screens and a bonus round. The broad platform list matters: publishers are treating the keyboard household as an arcade audience. The October notice does not pin either adaptation to a launch on this particular day.

stories.headline: A color printer for the home desk at $239
body: Okidata’s Okimate 10 promises full-color printing for Commodore and Atari home computers at an advertised $239. The October COMPUTE! product report says this thermal-transfer printer can put more than 40 shades onto ordinary paper or acetate.

At a specified 60 characters per second, it is hardly a pressroom machine. But its color output brings school projects, charts and home graphics a step closer to the modest computer desk. The advertised figure is a period list price, not a verified shop transaction this week.

stories.headline: IBM tries a second act for the PCjr
body: IBM’s repaired PCjr receives another look in October COMPUTE!: a typewriter-style keyboard replaces the original design, and existing owners are offered a free replacement. These changes were announced in July, not this week.

Snap-on 128K modules list for $325 apiece and can take the machine to 512K with three modules. The enhanced PCjr lists at $999, although the magazine saw a local $699 ComputerLand offer in early August. IBM also points to serious applications, including a planned Lotus 1-2-3 cartridge; its availability this week is not confirmed.

curiosity.headline: The Plus/4’s instant office has a 99-line ceiling
curiosity.summary: The built-in 3-Plus-1 word processor starts from ROM, yet Compute! reported a 99-line text limit.
curiosity.detail: The same review described horizontal scrolling to emulate a 77-column view, leaving a long sentence offscreen on the 40-column display.
